question.question: Regarding the decision not to recommend a specific chemical product or dosage, why should a farmer prioritize using AniCheck over simply waiting for an agricultural technician who can provide both the identification and a actionable treatment plan?

4. How acceptable is the developed application to its intended users when evaluated against the
ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics of functional suitability, usability, reliability, and portability?
Objectives of the Study
The general objective was to develop and evaluate a mobile application capable of identifying
common rice leaf diseases without requiring an internet connection. Specifically, the study aimed to
assemble a labeled image dataset of rice leaves representing four disease classes and a healthy class;
to train a convolutional neural network on that dataset using transfer learning; to convert and embed
the trained model in an Android application with an interface suitable for users with limited formal
schooling; and to evaluate both the classification performance of the model and the acceptability of
the application to its intended users.
Scope and Limitations
The application identifies four disease classes — bacterial leaf blight, brown spot, leaf smut, and
tungro — plus a healthy class. These four were selected because they were the diseases most
frequently named by farmers during the initial interviews and because they present visible foliar
symptoms. Diseases whose symptoms appear principally on the panicle, stem, or root, including
sheath blight and false smut, are outside the coverage of the system.
The image dataset was collected exclusively within Barangay Masagana during a six-week window
in the 2024 wet season. The application runs on Android 9.0 and above; no iOS version was
produced. The system returns an identification and a confidence percentage; it does not recommend
a specific chemical product or dosage, since the proponents judged that prescribing agricultural
chemicals falls outside both the competence of the development team and the intended function of a
diagnostic aid. The application is intended as a decision-support tool and not as a replacement for
consultation with a qualified agricultural technician.
Significance of the Study
For smallholder farmers, the study offers a means of obtaining a preliminary disease identification at
the moment of observation rather than at the next available consultation. For agricultural extension
officers, a tool that handles routine identification may allow scarce technician time to be directed
toward the cases that genuinely require expert judgment. For the local government unit, the
aggregate pattern of identifications could in principle inform the targeting of advisory campaigns,
although the present version of the system does not transmit or aggregate any data. For future
researchers, the study contributes a documented dataset collection procedure and a baseline set of
results against which alternative architectures may be compared.

turns.answer: Because the farmer usually can't wait for one. In our interviews, farmers saw a technician about once per cropping season, so 19 of the 24 relied on a neighbor or the supply store for a diagnosis, and 8 had applied a treatment that turned out to be wrong. AniCheck doesn't compete with the technician; it changes what happens at the moment the farmer first sees the symptom. It gives an identification and a confidence percentage on the phone, offline, so the farmer knows whether this looks like bacterial leaf blight or brown spot before buying anything. We left out chemicals and doses on purpose: prescribing pesticides is outside our competence, and a wrong dose after a misclassification costs more than no advice. So the app is the first step, and the Scope keeps the technician for the cases where a costly treatment follows.

Evaluation Design
Model performance was evaluated on the 648-image test set using accuracy, precision, recall, and
F1-score computed per class, together with a confusion matrix.
System acceptability was evaluated using a survey instrument adapted from ISO/IEC 25010,
covering four characteristics: functional suitability, usability, reliability, and portability. The
instrument consisted of twenty statements, five per characteristic, rated on a five-point Likert scale.
The instrument was translated into Filipino and reviewed for clarity by the adviser and by one
faculty member from the college.
Thirty respondents were selected through purposive sampling from among the rice farmers of
Barangay Masagana, the criteria being active cultivation of rice during the current season and
ownership of an Android smartphone. Each respondent attended a single session in which the
application was installed on their device, its use was demonstrated, and they were guided through
capturing between three and five identifications on leaves available at the session. Sessions ran
approximately thirty minutes. The survey was administered immediately afterward, with the
proponents reading each statement aloud and recording the response.
Responses were analyzed using weighted mean. The scale was interpreted according to the ranges in

Ethical Considerations
Permission to conduct the study within the barangay was obtained in writing from the barangay

discomfort with signing documents. No personally identifying information was recorded on the
survey forms, and the application stores identification history only on the user's own device.

turns.answer: We can't claim that, and I should correct my earlier answer. The 3,240 images came from eleven fields, but each leaf was detached and photographed on white cardboard between 8 and 10 AM, so occlusion, blur and glare were controlled out rather than measured. The 648 test images are a stratified 20% held out from that same collection, so the 94.7% is an in-distribution figure for detached leaves in morning light. The three to five captures in the evaluation sessions were never a dataset either; they only let each of the thirty respondents complete a full capture-and-identify cycle before rating the app. Our Limitations say the transfer to attached leaves and variable light was not established, and the study that would establish it is our recommendation to compare the app's calls with a technician's judgment on field leaves.

evaluation.primary_gap: The methodology admits to a complete lack of real-world environmental validation (occlusion, blur, dynamic lighting), rendering the field deployment aspect of the research largely theoretical.
evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate clarifies that the test dataset consisted of controlled, detached leaves in optimal lighting, admitting that the system's performance on attached leaves under variable field conditions was not established and remains a recommendation for future study.

next_question.question: I appreciate your candor regarding the discrepancy in model reliability, but if the respondents were fundamentally more confident in the application's usability than in its diagnostic accuracy, on what basis can you conclude that the system is a useful triage tool? If the primary users themselves express skepticism about the correctness of the findings, aren't you over-generalizing the clinical value of the system by labeling it as acceptable?

Discussion
The overall accuracy of 94.7% is lower than the figures commonly reported in the plant disease
classification literature, where results above 99% on the PlantVillage dataset are routine. The
proponents attribute the difference principally to dataset scale: 3,240 images across five classes is an
order of magnitude smaller than the datasets on which those figures were obtained.
The acceptability results indicate that the intended users found the system usable and useful. The
gap between the usability rating and the reliability rating is instructive: respondents were more
confident in their ability to operate the application than in the correctness of what it told them. For a
diagnostic tool this is the more consequential of the two dimensions, and it corresponds directly to
the per-class weakness identified on bacterial leaf blight.

next_question.grounding_reference: The gap between the usability rating and the reliability rating is instructive: respondents were more confident in their ability to operate the application than in the correctness of what it told them.

closing.line: My questions regarding the methodology of your data collection are complete.

turns.answer: We don't conclude it's a reliable diagnostic, and the reliability score is the reason. Reliability was the only ISO/IEC 25010 characteristic below Very Acceptable, at 4.09 against 4.42 for usability, and it lines up with the confusion matrix: bacterial leaf blight has the lowest recall, 0.813, with 16 of its 125 test images called brown spot, and several respondents' leaves carried more than one condition, which a single-class answer can't express. So the respondents' skepticism is consistent with the model's real weakness, not a contradiction of it. That's why the conclusion is narrow: the app is acceptable as a preliminary identification aid that is easy to use offline, and it should not replace a technician where a costly treatment follows. 'Acceptable' there is the ISO rating of the app as a whole, not a claim of clinical accuracy.

evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate argues that the app's 'acceptable' status refers to its utility as a preliminary aid rather than clinical diagnostic accuracy, and posits that user skepticism regarding reliability is a logical reflection of the system's known multi-class limitations.

closing.line: Those are all the inquiries I have regarding your conclusions and the scope of your findings.

turns.answer: We don't claim field suitability for the model's accuracy; the functional suitability rating is what thirty farmers reported after using the app, and it measures whether the features did what they expected, not field accuracy. The design deliberately keeps a misdiagnosis from turning straight into a chemical application: the app shows an identification with a confidence percentage and never a product or a dose, and the Scope keeps the technician for any costly treatment. What's not established is how the 94.7% holds on attached leaves in field light, and we say so in the Limitations. Until the field validation in our recommendations is done, the honest reading is a preliminary aid that narrows what the farmer asks the technician, not a substitute for one.

evaluation.primary_gap: The candidate admits the functional suitability rating is based on guided, non-field conditions, which calls into question the validity of using that metric to claim real-world system utility.
evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate clarifies that functional suitability ratings were based on user experience surveys rather than field accuracy, and acknowledges that the system is intended as a preliminary diagnostic aid requiring expert verification rather than a replacement for field technicians.

report.narrative:
You have now completed your defense session, which saw a fluctuating difficulty trajectory across six turns. Your performance metrics reflect an overall average clarity of 80, a depth of 70, and grounding of 77.

The session was marked by two significant pushback events. At turn two, the panel increased the difficulty from a level 2 to a level 3, during which your response quality deteriorated compared to your previous turn. However, you demonstrated resilience during the second pushback at turn four; after the difficulty escalated back to level 3, your response quality recovered, matching the performance level you held prior to the challenge.

Reviewing the feedback by panelist, O'Sullivan noted that you cited statistics absent from your stated methodology. Zimmermann highlighted that your reliance on non-field condition testing undermines your claims regarding real-world system utility. Most critically, Nguyen identified significant gaps in your experimental rigor, specifically regarding the representativeness of your dataset, the lack of formal methodology for dataset validation, and the absence of real-world environmental validation. These critiques suggest that your field deployment conclusions currently remain largely theoretical. While you achieved strong clarity and depth scores with Abara, addressing the methodological concerns raised by Nguyen will be essential for the future development of your research.

transcript.answer: We can't claim that, and I should correct my earlier answer. The 3,240 images came from eleven fields, but each leaf was detached and photographed on white cardboard between 8 and 10 AM, so occlusion, blur and glare were controlled out rather than measured. The 648 test images are a stratified 20% held out from that same collection, so the 94.7% is an in-distribution figure for detached leaves in morning light. The three to five captures in the evaluation sessions were never a dataset either; they only let each of the thirty respondents complete a full capture-and-identify cycle before rating the app. Our Limitations say the transfer to attached leaves and variable light was not established, and the study that would establish it is our recommendation to compare the app's calls with a technician's judgment on field leaves.

Discussion
The overall accuracy of 94.7% is lower than the figures commonly reported in the plant disease
classification literature, where results above 99% on the PlantVillage dataset are routine. The
proponents attribute the difference principally to dataset scale: 3,240 images across five classes is an
order of magnitude smaller than the datasets on which those figures were obtained.
The acceptability results indicate that the intended users found the system usable and useful. The
gap between the usability rating and the reliability rating is instructive: respondents were more
confident in their ability to operate the application than in the correctness of what it told them. For a
diagnostic tool this is the more consequential of the two dimensions, and it corresponds directly to
the per-class weakness identified on bacterial leaf blight.

transcript.grounding_reference: The gap between the usability rating and the reliability rating is instructive: respondents were more confident in their ability to operate the application than in the correctness of what it told them.
transcript.answer: We don't conclude it's a reliable diagnostic, and the reliability score is the reason. Reliability was the only ISO/IEC 25010 characteristic below Very Acceptable, at 4.09 against 4.42 for usability, and it lines up with the confusion matrix: bacterial leaf blight has the lowest recall, 0.813, with 16 of its 125 test images called brown spot, and several respondents' leaves carried more than one condition, which a single-class answer can't express. So the respondents' skepticism is consistent with the model's real weakness, not a contradiction of it. That's why the conclusion is narrow: the app is acceptable as a preliminary identification aid that is easy to use offline, and it should not replace a technician where a costly treatment follows. 'Acceptable' there is the ISO rating of the app as a whole, not a claim of clinical accuracy.

evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate argues that the app's 'acceptable' status refers to its utility as a preliminary aid rather than clinical diagnostic accuracy, and posits that user skepticism regarding reliability is a logical reflection of the system's known multi-class limitations.

closing.line: Those are all the inquiries I have regarding your conclusions and the scope of your findings.

Evaluation Design
Model performance was evaluated on the 648-image test set using accuracy, precision, recall, and
F1-score computed per class, together with a confusion matrix.
System acceptability was evaluated using a survey instrument adapted from ISO/IEC 25010,
covering four characteristics: functional suitability, usability, reliability, and portability. The
instrument consisted of twenty statements, five per characteristic, rated on a five-point Likert scale.
The instrument was translated into Filipino and reviewed for clarity by the adviser and by one
faculty member from the college.
Thirty respondents were selected through purposive sampling from among the rice farmers of
Barangay Masagana, the criteria being active cultivation of rice during the current season and
ownership of an Android smartphone. Each respondent attended a single session in which the
application was installed on their device, its use was demonstrated, and they were guided through
capturing between three and five identifications on leaves available at the session. Sessions ran
approximately thirty minutes. The survey was administered immediately afterward, with the
proponents reading each statement aloud and recording the response.

transcript.answer: We don't claim field suitability for the model's accuracy; the functional suitability rating is what thirty farmers reported after using the app, and it measures whether the features did what they expected, not field accuracy. The design deliberately keeps a misdiagnosis from turning straight into a chemical application: the app shows an identification with a confidence percentage and never a product or a dose, and the Scope keeps the technician for any costly treatment. What's not established is how the 94.7% holds on attached leaves in field light, and we say so in the Limitations. Until the field validation in our recommendations is done, the honest reading is a preliminary aid that narrows what the farmer asks the technician, not a substitute for one.

evaluation.primary_gap: The candidate admits the functional suitability rating is based on guided, non-field conditions, which calls into question the validity of using that metric to claim real-world system utility.
evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate clarifies that functional suitability ratings were based on user experience surveys rather than field accuracy, and acknowledges that the system is intended as a preliminary diagnostic aid requiring expert verification rather than a replacement for field technicians.
